steps.html:
In fluent speech, words run into one another and half the small ones disappear. This lesson is about hearing what was actually said — and about the communities that now exist only on a screen.

  • Work out what was said when words run together
  • Follow a talk on online and virtual communities
  • Use high-frequency verb collocations: get support, give permission
  • Write about an online community you belong to

Help and encouragement. You get, give, offer or need support.

To change slightly, or to get used to a new situation. Adjust to something.

steps.title: Before you listen: why is fluent English hard to catch?
options: Words run into one another, so the gaps between them disappear.
Fluent speakers leave out the main verbs.
steps.answer: Words run into one another, so the gaps between them disappear.
steps.why: Written English has a space between every word. Spoken English does not, which is why who is can arrive as one sound.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: The speaker opens by describing what we usually picture — people living close to each other — before turning to online communities.
steps.prompt: Why begin with the idea she is about to set aside?
options: Because she thinks the traditional kind is more important.
Because the contrast makes the point: the same word now covers something the listener was not picturing.
Because she is unsure which definition to use.
steps.answer: Because the contrast makes the point: the same word now covers something the listener was not picturing.
steps.why: The talk is about a word whose meaning has moved. She has to establish the old meaning before the movement is visible.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: In the recording, 'Users can set up their own courses' is very hard to catch, although every word in it is common.
steps.prompt: Why?
options: Because the speaker reaches for unusual vocabulary at exactly that point.
Because the words run together and the unstressed ones almost disappear, so the boundaries have to be worked out rather than heard.
Because the recording quality drops for a second or two there.
steps.answer: Because the words run together and the unstressed ones almost disappear, so the boundaries have to be worked out rather than heard.
steps.why: Difficulty in fluent speech is almost never lexical. It is where one word ends and the next begins.

steps.title: The small words that are already fixed for you
steps.html:
Recycled from Lessons 13 and 14, and now inside the fixed phrases that carry them.

A great deal of B2 accuracy is not choice at all — it is a fixed phrase you either know or do not. Get support takes no article. Give permission takes no article. Carry out research takes no article, and never a plural.

The nouns that trip learners up here are the ones that look countable but are not: research, support, advice, information, permission, equipment, homework. None of them takes a, and none of them has a plural.

To count them, use a partitive: a piece of research, a piece of advice, a great deal of support, an item of equipment.

The quantifiers from Lesson 14 sort themselves accordingly: much research but many courses; a little support but a few members; a great deal of information but a great many people.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences from the talk and the texts in this unit.

People with a rare illness can now get support from others.
No article.

According to recent research, the number is rising.
Uncountable, no article, no plural.

Neighbours give each other permission to borrow things.
No article.

Anyone can join in an educational course.
Countable → an.

Many of these communities cross international borders.
Countable plural + of these.

Plenty of them have a serious purpose.
Countable plural.

They offer to lend things like barbecue equipment.
Uncountable, no plural.

A great deal of support comes from complete strangers.
Uncountable quantifier.

A great many members have never met.
Countable quantifier.

She gave me a piece of advice I still use.
Partitive to make an uncountable countable.

steps.title: Fixing a sentence with an uncountable noun
steps.html:
1. The sentence a learner wrote: She gave me an advice and a lot of supports.
  2. Advice is uncountable, so an is impossible. Either drop it — She gave me advice — or add a partitive: a piece of advice.
  3. Support is uncountable, so it has no plural. A lot of support is correct; supports is not.
  4. Check the quantifier matches: a lot of works with both, so it can stay.
  5. Result: She gave me a piece of advice and a lot of support.

steps.title: You are going to write about an online community.
steps.sub: Choose the one you will write about.

options.label: One you have only read about
One that helped somebody you know

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Say what it is for, who is in it, and what it actually gives people.
steps.placeholder: The community I belong to is …
steps.html:
• Say what the community is and who is in it.
  • Say what people go there for.
  • Say what they actually get, which is usually something else.
  • Include one figure and describe it with an adverb.
  • Check every uncountable noun.

Useful language

  • It is an online community for people who …
  • Members get support / advice / information from …
  • A great many of them have never met in person.
  • According to recent research, …
  • The number has risen significantly / dramatically since …
  • What it really provides is …
steps.modelHtml:
Four hundred people and one broken washing machine

The community I belong to is a forum for people who repair old domestic appliances. It has around four hundred active members and a great many more who read without posting. A few of them are professional engineers. Most are not.

You go there for information — a wiring diagram, a part number, a photograph of the inside of a machine nobody has made since 1994. What you get is more than that. Members will spend an evening writing out an explanation for somebody they will never meet, and nobody is paid anything.

According to recent research, this kind of group is the fastest-growing form of community there is, and the numbers have risen dramatically since 2015. I can see why. It is the only place I have ever been given a piece of advice that was both free and correct.
